docs.title: Vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting — From Initialization to a Trained Scene
docs.text:
An implementation-aware, visual, mathematical, and interactive tutorial using an indoor-scene reconstruction.

Before you start

Prerequisites: Computer Vision Fundamentals explains cameras, COLMAP, radiance, and general CV vocabulary. 3DGS Fundamentals introduces Gaussian primitives, opacity, covariance, and splatting. This page explains how the original Vanilla 3DGS algorithm actually works, without re-teaching the prerequisites.

Audience: ML practitioners learning 3D reconstruction. Equations are accompanied by operational explanations and interactive exercises. The examples use the official Inria 3DGS implementation; defaults can differ across versions and forks.

Jump to: Pipeline · Initialization · Gaussian parameters · Projection · SH color · Tiles · Compositing · Loss · Densification · PLY · Experiments.

docs.title: 1. The complete pipeline
docs.text:
At training time:

  1. Estimate camera intrinsics, poses, and sparse points with COLMAP (or another compatible reconstruction method).
  2. Create an initial trainable 3D Gaussian for each seed point.
  3. Select a training camera and render its predicted RGB image from all relevant Gaussians.
  4. Compare the rendering with that camera's fixed reference photograph.
  5. Backpropagate the image loss through the differentiable rasterizer; update Gaussian parameters with an optimizer.
  6. Periodically clone, split, and prune Gaussians according to prescribed density-control rules.
  7. Save a set of trained Gaussians; later, supply a camera to render another view.

The key mental model: a Gaussian is a persistent 3D primitive. An image is a temporary result computed from thousands of such primitives for one camera. Training adjusts the primitives, not independent pixels.

docs.title: A concrete indoor-scene example
docs.text:
For the indoor scene used throughout these notes, the sparse COLMAP reconstruction provided 38,558 initial points, and the trained 30,000-iteration Vanilla 3DGS PLY contains 637,141 Gaussians. These are real counts from this specific experiment, not universal benchmarks. The number grew because densification can create extra primitives during training.

Iteration is not epoch

One training iteration selects a camera view and updates the scene. An epoch normally means a pass through a dataset. A 30,000-iteration run is not 30,000 epochs.

docs.title: 2. From COLMAP points to trainable Gaussians
docs.text: COLMAP provides camera calibration/poses, registered photographs, and sparse 3D points. The 3DGS model is constructed after that reconstruction. It does not inherit a ready-made set of optimized Gaussians from COLMAP.

docs.title: What exactly gets initialized?
docs.text:
Gaussian attribute Typical official initialization Why Center \(\boldsymbol\mu\) A sparse COLMAP 3D point Put initial primitives in plausible scene locations SH color (degree 0) Transform the seed point's RGB color to the constant SH coefficient Start with approximate observed appearance Higher-order SH color Zeros Let training discover view-dependent color Three scales Isotropic initial spread estimated from neighbor-point distances Give seed points finite extent Rotation Identity quaternion Begin without an arbitrary orientation Activated opacity \(0.1\) (stored as logit) Allow compositing and opacity learning

These values are starting points, not final properties. Subsequent optimization can move the centers, flatten or elongate the Gaussians, rotate them, and alter opacity and color.

The reference implementation computes approximate squared nearest-neighbor distances with simple-knn, clamps small values, and initializes each log-scale using \(\log\sqrt{d_i^2}\). Its initial rotation is \((1,0,0,0)\), and the initial opacity parameter is \(\operatorname{logit}(0.1)\). Source: scene/gaussian_model.py.

Not one Gaussian per photograph pixel

Seed Gaussians correspond to 3D sparse points, not the pixels of any particular image. A single persistent Gaussian can be observed at different screen coordinates in many cameras.

docs.title: 3. Gaussian parameters and 3D covariance
docs.text: A trained Gaussian has a center \(\boldsymbol\mu\), three scale parameters, a rotation quaternion, opacity, and SH appearance coefficients. These are different trainable quantities with different effects on the rendering.

docs.title: Stored parameters versus activated values
docs.text:
Stored in PLY Conversion for rendering Meaning x, y, z Used directly World-space Gaussian center scale_0, scale_1, scale_2 \(s_k=\exp(\tilde s_k)\) Positive directional standard deviations rot_0 ... rot_3 Normalize quaternion \(q/\lVert q\rVert\) Ellipsoid orientation opacity \(o=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\tilde o)\) Base opacity in \((0,1)\) f_dc_*, f_rest_* Evaluate spherical harmonics View-dependent RGB appearance

Let \(R(q)\) denote the rotation matrix of the normalized quaternion. Then

\[ \boxed{\boldsymbol\Sigma_{3D}=R(q)\operatorname{diag}(s_x^2,s_y^2,s_z^2)R(q)^\top.} \]

A spatial Gaussian's influence at location \(\mathbf x\) is often visualized using

\[ G(\mathbf x)=\exp\!\left[-\frac12(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{3D}^{-1}(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)\right]. \]

Its ellipsoidal level surfaces are not hard physical boundaries. The three activated scales control thickness and stretching in local directions; rotation controls those directions in world space; opacity controls the strength of the subsequent splat.

Practical mental picture: a broad, thin Gaussian can approximate part of a chair seat; a narrow, elongated Gaussian can approximate a leg. These are scene approximations, not object labels or physically rigid pieces.

docs.title: 4. Projecting a 3D Gaussian to 2D
docs.text: This is the bridge from the 3D representation to the 2D image. We calculate a screen-space center and a screen-space shape for a Gaussian at a selected camera.

docs.title: 4.1 Project the Gaussian center
docs.text:
After applying the world-to-camera transform, let the center be \(\boldsymbol\mu_c=(X,Y,Z)^\top\). Under an ideal pinhole camera,

\[ \mathbf m_{2D}=\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix}f_x X/Z+c_x\\ f_yY/Z+c_y\end{bmatrix}. \]

For example, \(f_x=600\), \(X=1\), \(Z=5\), \(c_x=320\) gives \(u=440\) pixels. That is the projected center, not the complete footprint. Camera conventions and intrinsic assumptions are explained in CV Fundamentals.

docs.title: 4.2 Project its shape, not just its center
docs.text:
Let \(W\) be the rotational part of the world-to-camera transform and \(J\) the Jacobian of the perspective projection evaluated at \(\boldsymbol\mu_c\):

\[ J=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{f_x}{Z} & 0 & -\frac{f_x X}{Z^2}\\ 0 & \frac{f_y}{Z} & -\frac{f_y Y}{Z^2} \end{bmatrix}. \]

A first-order approximation to the projected \(2\times2\) covariance is

\[ \boxed{\boldsymbol\Sigma_{2D}\approx JW\boldsymbol\Sigma_{3D}W^\top J^\top.} \]

The rasterizer also handles practical filtering and numerical details; the reference implementation adds a small screen-space low-pass term to the covariance. The resulting footprint depends on the camera: a Gaussian can look long from one angle and nearly circular from another.

docs.title: 4.3 Turn the 2D covariance into a pixel contribution
docs.text:
Write the difference between pixel center \(\mathbf p\) and projected center as \(\boldsymbol\delta=\mathbf p-\mathbf m_{2D}\). The footprint weight is approximately

\[ w(\mathbf p)=\exp\!\left(-\frac12\boldsymbol\delta^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{2D}^{-1}\boldsymbol\delta\right), \qquad \alpha(\mathbf p)=\min\{0.99,\;o\,w(\mathbf p)\}. \]

The real rasterizer also culls extremely small contributions. The same Gaussian can influence several adjacent pixels with different effective alpha values.

docs.title: Try it: Move a Gaussian relative to a camera
docs.text:
Open projection explorer separately.

The explorer is pedagogical rather than a reproduction of every CUDA covariance/clamping detail.

docs.title: 5. Spherical harmonics: view-dependent appearance
docs.text:
A Gaussian has one location, scale, rotation, and set of SH coefficients; those stored parameters do not change merely because we move the camera. Yet the color evaluated from its SH coefficients can change with the viewing direction.

For a unit direction \(\mathbf d=(d_x,d_y,d_z)\) pointing from the camera toward the Gaussian, the degree-3 SH color uses 16 real basis functions for each RGB channel:

\[ \boxed{\mathbf c(\mathbf d)=\max\!\left(\mathbf 0,\;\frac12\mathbf 1+ \sum_{k=0}^{15}Y_k(\mathbf d)\,\mathbf a_k\right).} \]
  • \(Y_k\) is a fixed direction-dependent basis function.
  • \(\mathbf a_k\in\mathbb R^3\) is a learned coefficient for R, G, and B.
  • Degree 0 uses one coefficient per channel (the constant component).
  • Degree 3 uses 16 coefficients per channel, or 48 appearance values per Gaussian.

The constant coefficient is learned from point RGB at initialization; the remaining 45 coefficients start at zero. The official trainer starts with active degree 0 and increases the active SH degree at intervals of 1,000 iterations, until the configured maximum (typically 3). Source: train.py.

docs.title: Worked first-order example
docs.text:
For one color channel and just two illustrative basis terms, imagine

\[c(\mathbf d)=0.5 + a_0 Y_0 + a_1Y_1(\mathbf d).\]

Moving the camera changes \(Y_1(\mathbf d)\) while \(a_0\) and \(a_1\) remain fixed. This is how a trained Gaussian can change its apparent color across viewpoints without storing separate RGB values for every camera.

docs.title: Interactive experiment: view direction and apparent color
docs.text:
A one-channel first-order SH teaching model

Rotate the viewing direction. The plotted color intensity changes from a fixed set of illustrative coefficients; the Gaussian's parameters do not change.

Viewing angle: 0° —Toy expression: intensity = clamp(0.55 + 0.30 cos(angle), 0, 1).

This shows **directional dependence**, not the actual learned coefficients in your PLY. Use the real-data notebook below to inspect trained SH values.

Color is not opacity

SH supplies a Gaussian's RGB value for the current camera direction. The projected spatial footprint and opacity determine how strongly that color enters each pixel, after accounting for nearer Gaussians.

docs.title: 6. Tile-based rasterization: how the GPU finds the relevant Gaussians
docs.text:
Imagine an image of size \(64\times64\) pixels. The reference rasterizer processes it as a grid of \(16\times16\)-pixel tiles: there are \(4\times4=16\) tiles. For a full-resolution image, there can be many more tiles.

A naive renderer would test every Gaussian against every pixel. The tile-based rasterizer avoids most unnecessary tests.

docs.title: The actual steps
docs.text:
1. Project the Gaussian center and covariance to the current camera, estimate a bounded screen-space footprint, and cull irrelevant Gaussians.
  2. Find its overlapping tile rectangle. If its footprint bounds overlap tiles T5 and T6, both tiles record the Gaussian's ID.
  3. Emit references, not new Gaussians. A single Gaussian may appear in several tile lists; this is not densification.
  4. Sort by tile ID and camera depth. The code constructs a combined sort key containing the tile and the Gaussian-center depth.
  5. Create a list range for each tile, then have the pixel-processing GPU threads read that tile's ordered Gaussian references.
  6. For each pixel, evaluate spatial weights and alpha, and blend contributions front to back.

The depth ordering uses Gaussian-center depth, which is an approximation rather than an independent exact surface ordering at each pixel. Relevant reference CUDA functions include duplicateWithKeys, identifyTileRanges, and renderCUDA in the differentiable rasterizer.

docs.title: Interactive experiment: tile coverage
docs.text:
Move the Gaussian's screen-space footprint over the tile grid

The blue tiles receive a **reference to this Gaussian** because its conservative bounding rectangle overlaps them.

Gaussian center x: 25 px Gaussian center y: 25 px Bounding radius: 13 px —— Reset

This diagram uses a circular outline for visibility and a square bounding box for tile assignment. An actual 2D Gaussian can be elliptical; the CUDA implementation computes conservative pixel bounds using its projected covariance.

docs.title: Numerical tile example
docs.text:
Suppose Gaussian G7 projects to \((25,25)\) with a 13-pixel bounding radius. Its rectangle spans approximately pixels 12–38 horizontally and vertically, crossing tile columns 0, 1, and 2 and tile rows 0, 1, and 2. Thus G7 appears in nine tile lists. There is still only one Gaussian G7 in the 3D scene.

Now tile T5 might contain G7 (depth 2), G12 (depth 5), and G4 (depth 8). The rasterizer sorts the references in that order for the tile. It does not sort by a semantic label or by Gaussian color.

docs.title: 7. Visibility and alpha compositing
docs.text:
Tile sorting brings each pixel a candidate list. The pixel then determines each Gaussian's actual opacity at its location and combines the colors in front-to-back order.

For pixel \(\mathbf p\), let \(\alpha_i(\mathbf p)\) be Gaussian \(i\)'s effective alpha, \(\mathbf c_i\) its evaluated SH color, and \(T_i\) the transmittance remaining before that Gaussian:

\[ T_1=1,\qquad T_i(\mathbf p)=\prod_{j<i}(1-\alpha_j(\mathbf p)). \]

Then the rendered RGB value, including remaining background, is

\[ \boxed{\hat{\mathbf C}(\mathbf p)= \sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i(\mathbf p)\alpha_i(\mathbf p)\mathbf c_i +T_{N+1}(\mathbf p)\mathbf c_{\mathrm{bg}}.} \]

docs.title: Worked example: red in front of blue
docs.text:
A near red Gaussian has \(\alpha_1=0.6\) and \(\mathbf c_1=(1,0,0)\). A farther blue one has \(\alpha_2=0.5\) and \(\mathbf c_2=(0,0,1)\). With a black background,

\[ \hat{\mathbf C}=0.6(1,0,0)+(1-0.6)\cdot0.5(0,0,1)=(0.6,0,0.2). \]

Why is the blue contribution only 0.2? The front Gaussian leaves transmittance \(T_2=1-0.6=0.4\), so its effective contribution is \(0.4\times0.5=0.2\). Rear objects cannot contribute at full strength through an already opaque foreground.

docs.title: Try it: interactive compositing
docs.text:
Open the compositing explorer separately.

Distinguish these three: an SH color is an RGB value evaluated from a direction; base opacity is a learned Gaussian parameter; effective alpha varies by pixel due to the Gaussian's projected footprint. They are combined through transmittance.

docs.title: 8. RGB reconstruction loss and backpropagation
docs.text:
This section integrates our formerly separate Vanilla 3DGS Loss Function tutorial, including both of its interactive labs. Readers can follow the loss calculation without switching pages.

Core training objective

The baseline Vanilla 3DGS RGB objective combines L1 image reconstruction and SSIM structural similarity. The default mixing weight is \(\lambda=0.2\). Some newer repository versions additionally support optional depth regularization, which is separate from the basic RGB objective and only applies when configured and valid depth supervision is available.

docs.title: 8.1. What is compared with what?
docs.text:
Imagine a photograph of a chair in an indoor room. COLMAP has estimated the camera pose of that photograph. We use that same camera to render the current Gaussian scene.

Figure: Vanilla 3DGS RGB reconstruction training pipeline. A rendered image is compared with the reference photograph from the same camera viewpoint. The loss is backpropagated through the differentiable renderer to update Gaussian parameters.

Let the original photograph be \(I_v\) and the rendered photograph be \(\hat I_v\) for camera view \(v\). They have the same image dimensions, and pixel \((x,y)\) of one corresponds to pixel \((x,y)\) of the other.

  • Original image \(I_v\): fixed training target; its RGB values are not updated.
  • Rendered image \(\hat I_v\): computed from the current trainable Gaussian scene and camera.
  • Pixelwise difference: measures a mismatch in image space, not a distance between 3D points.

The renderer is a function of the Gaussian parameters \(\theta\) and the known camera \(\mathcal C_v\):

\[\hat I_v=\mathcal R(\theta,\mathcal C_v)\]

Each Gaussian has a 3D mean (position), a covariance (shape and orientation), an opacity parameter, and view-dependent color parameters represented with spherical harmonics. Their combined projections and alpha compositing produce the rendered RGB image.

docs.title: 8.2. Interactive lab: Compare a reference image with a rendering
docs.text:
In this miniature illustrative indoor scene, a chair has the wrong brightness and horizontal position in the rendered image. Move the controls and observe three images: the fixed reference, the current rendering, and a pixelwise error visualization.

Important: This lab draws a small synthetic image to illustrate the RGB comparison. It is not a full 3D Gaussian rasterizer. The loss functions, however, are computed from the actual image arrays, including a windowed SSIM calculation.

Interactive experiment A · RGB reconstruction A small indoor photograph

The original is fixed. Change the simulated rendering to see how two standard loss components respond. Click any pixel to inspect its RGB values.

Reference imageFixed training target Rendered imageCurrent Gaussian scene (analogy) Absolute differenceBrighter red = larger RGB error Rendered chair brightness 65% Rendered chair horizontal offset +2 px SSIM loss weight (λ) 0.20 Mean RGB L1— 1 − SSIM— Combined loss— Select a pixel on one of the images to compare its RGB values. Match the reference chairReset experiment

All RGB values are normalized to [0, 1] for loss calculation. SSIM uses 11×11 Gaussian-weighted neighborhoods (σ = 1.5), constants C₁ = 0.01² and C₂ = 0.03², and zero-padding as in the original software SSIM implementation. This tiny test image is only for learning, so numerical SSIM values are not representative of a full-resolution dataset.

Enable JavaScript to use the interactive comparison. The mathematical explanation below remains available without JavaScript.

docs.title: The first loss: Mean absolute RGB error (L1)
docs.text:
For RGB images of height \(H\) and width \(W\), mean L1 is:

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RGB}\text{-}L1}=\frac{1}{3HW}\sum_{y=1}^{H}\sum_{x=1}^{W}\sum_{c\in\{R,G,B\}}\left|I_v(y,x,c)-\hat I_v(y,x,c)\right|\]

The images are normalized to \([0,1]\). For example, for a single RGB pixel:

Channel Original (0–255) Rendered (0–255) Absolute error Red 200 170 30 Green 160 140 20 Blue 120 100 20

Its mean absolute channel error is \((30+20+20)/(3\times255)\approx0.0915\) after normalization. Real training averages this error across every pixel in the selected training image.

L1 is easy to interpret, but independently matching color values does not fully express whether the image has the right local patterns and structure. That motivates the second term.

docs.title: The second loss: Structural similarity (SSIM)
docs.text:
SSIM compares local neighborhoods of corresponding images. In each local window it uses brightness statistics, contrast statistics, and covariance (how pixel variations agree).

For two local image windows \(x\) and \(y\):

\[\operatorname{SSIM}(x,y)=\frac{(2\mu_x\mu_y+C_1)(2\sigma_{xy}+C_2)}{(\mu_x^2+\mu_y^2+C_1)(\sigma_x^2+\sigma_y^2+C_2)}\]

where \(\mu_x,\mu_y\) are local means; \(\sigma_x^2,\sigma_y^2\) are local variances; \(\sigma_{xy}\) is local covariance. The original 3DGS loss utility uses an 11×11 Gaussian window with \(\sigma=1.5\), \(C_1=0.01^2\), \(C_2=0.03^2\), and averages the SSIM map over image pixels and channels.

  • A perfect match has SSIM = 1, hence 1 − SSIM = 0.
  • Blurred edges, displaced structures, or incorrect local contrast usually decrease SSIM.
  • The training objective therefore minimizes \(1-\operatorname{SSIM}\) rather than maximizing SSIM directly.

Explore the distinction

In the image lab, first set the chair brightness to 100% but leave its horizontal position offset. Then set the offset to 0. Watch how a structural misalignment affects both L1 and SSIM even when the chair's RGB values are otherwise correct.

docs.title: 8.3. Combining L1 and SSIM
docs.text:
The core RGB reconstruction objective in original vanilla 3DGS is:

\[\boxed{\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RGB}}=(1-\lambda)\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RGB}\text{-}L1}+\lambda\,\bigl(1-\operatorname{SSIM}(\hat I_v,I_v)\bigr)}\]

With the default \(\lambda=0.2\):

\[\boxed{\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RGB}}=0.8\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RGB}\text{-}L1}+0.2\,(1-\operatorname{SSIM})}\]

You can adjust \(\lambda\) in the interactive lab. The combined loss is a scalar, but it was computed from many individual image differences. Its derivative with respect to all trainable Gaussians is obtained using automatic differentiation through the renderer.

Scope of the equation

This page explains the original RGB photometric objective. More recent versions of the official implementation can optionally add inverse-depth regularization when suitable depth supervision is available. That extra term is not part of the simple two-term RGB objective explained here.

docs.title: 8.4. How a pixel's error reaches a Gaussian
docs.text:
A pixel itself is not a trainable variable. The pixel value results from projected Gaussian footprints, their colors, visibility, and front-to-back alpha compositing.

For a pixel \(p\), the renderer can be written schematically as:

\[\hat{\mathbf C}(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i(p)\,\alpha_i(p)\,\mathbf c_i(p)+T_{N+1}(p)\,\mathbf c_{\mathrm{bg}},\qquad T_i(p)=\prod_{j Here, Gaussians are ordered front-to-back **for that camera view**; \\(\alpha_i(p)\\) is the effective pixel opacity (learned opacity multiplied by the 2D Gaussian footprint); \\(T_i(p)\\) is accumulated transmittance; \\(\mathbf c_i(p)\\) is the Gaussian's possibly view-dependent RGB color. For one grayscale pixel with just **two** front-to-back Gaussians, this reduces to: \[\hat C=\alpha_1c_1+(1-\alpha_1)\alpha_2c_2+(1-\alpha_1)(1-\alpha_2)c_{\mathrm{bg}}\] In the next interactive lab, each color is one grayscale number. The background is fixed at 0.10, and we use a target pixel of 0.75. Move the sliders to see how a *single pixel error* depends on multiple Gaussian parameters. Interactive experiment B · Backpropagation intuition One pixel produced by two Gaussians

Gaussian 1 is in front of Gaussian 2. Adjust their effective pixel opacities and grayscale colors. The target is fixed at 0.75.

G₁ effective opacity (α₁) 0.60 G₁ grayscale color (c₁) 0.45 G₂ effective opacity (α₂) 0.50 G₂ grayscale color (c₂) 0.90 Target grayscale Rendered grayscale Rendered: 0.470L1: 0.280 Contributions to the rendered pixel G₁: 0.270 + G₂: 0.180 + background: 0.020 = 0.470 L1 gradients, holding opacities fixed ∂L/∂c₁ = −0.600; ∂L/∂c₂ = −0.200 Apply one toy SGD step (colors only)Reset

This applies an illustrative SGD step with learning rate 0.2 to two grayscale color values using one-pixel L1 gradients. Actual 3DGS uses many RGB pixels, view-dependent colors, full rasterizer derivatives, parameter-specific learning rates, and Adam-style optimization. It does not use this toy update rule.

#### Why the two Gaussian colors receive different gradients In the simplified two-Gaussian pixel: \[\frac{\partial\hat C}{\partial c_1}=\alpha_1,\qquad\frac{\partial\hat C}{\partial c_2}=(1-\alpha_1)\alpha_2\] For the single-pixel L1 loss \\(L=|\hat C-C_{\mathrm{target}}|\\), away from an exact match: \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial c_i}=\operatorname{sign}(\hat C-C_{\mathrm{target}})\frac{\partial\hat C}{\partial c_i}\] This is the **chain rule**. The pixel error affects both Gaussians but in proportion to how strongly their color values influence the rendered pixel. In a full image, a Gaussian may contribute to hundreds of pixels. Its total gradient accumulates the derivatives from **all relevant pixel losses**. Position, covariance, and opacity also receive gradients through their effect on projected footprints and compositing weights. **No Gaussian is assigned permanently to one pixel.** The same 3D Gaussian projects into different image regions for different camera viewpoints. ### 8.5. End-to-end training through the loss 1. **Select a known training camera** and its original photograph. Camera parameters come from the reconstruction (such as COLMAP). 2. **Project visible 3D Gaussians** into that camera view. Their 3D positions/covariances determine screen-space footprints and the visibility order. 3. **Rasterize and alpha-composite** the Gaussians into a rendered RGB image \\(\hat I_v\\). 4. **Compute loss:** mean RGB L1 and local SSIM against the original image \\(I_v\\), weighted 0.8 and 0.2 by default. 5. **Backpropagate:** automatic differentiation computes \\(\nabla_\theta\mathcal L\\) through the rendering computation. 6. **Update Gaussian parameters:** the optimizer uses those gradients to change the learned parameters, subject to their learning rates and optimizer states. 7. **Repeat from other camera views.** Many distinct observations constrain the same shared 3D scene. A mathematical summary is: \[\theta\longrightarrow\hat I_v=\mathcal R(\theta,\mathcal C_v)\longrightarrow\mathcal L(\hat I_v,I_v)\longrightarrow\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal L\longrightarrow\theta_{\mathrm{updated}}\] The toy examples use gradient descent for transparency. In real training, vanilla 3DGS uses adaptive optimization (typically Adam). The optimizer's update depends not only on the current gradient but also on its accumulated optimizer statistics. #### Densification is a separate operation Gradient descent changes attributes of existing Gaussians. **Densification** can additionally clone or split Gaussians where reconstruction would benefit from more representation capacity, while pruning removes unhelpful Gaussians. These are part of the broader training algorithm, but **they are not additional terms in the core RGB loss equation**. ### 8.6. Frequently confused ideas | Question | Correct mental model | |---|---| | Is loss computed in 3D? | The **RGB loss is evaluated in 2D image space**; gradients then update 3D scene parameters. | | Does each pixel have one Gaussian? | No. A pixel can combine several Gaussians, and each Gaussian may cover many pixels. | | Does the model directly change pixel colors? | No. It changes the **Gaussian parameters** that produce those pixels when rendered. | | Is the original image updated? | No. It is the fixed ground-truth target for that training view. | | Are L1 and SSIM separate training passes? | No. They contribute to **one combined differentiable loss** for the rendered image. | | Is PSNR another training loss in vanilla 3DGS? | Normally **no**. PSNR is primarily a reconstruction-quality evaluation metric. | | Does one low-loss training image prove a correct 3D reconstruction? | No. Accurate **novel views and held-out camera views** are needed to judge whether the shared scene generalizes. | ### 8.7. Check your understanding Question 1. If a rendered chair pixel is too dark, which parameter is updated: the pixel or the Gaussians?

The **Gaussians**. Backpropagation computes how their colors, opacities, projected positions, and other trainable parameters affect that pixel and the rest of the image.

Question 2. Why can one Gaussian receive gradients from several different pixels?

Because the Gaussian's projected footprint contributes to a region of the image. Its parameter changes can alter all those pixels simultaneously.

Question 3. If the chair's color is correct but its rendered silhouette is displaced, should the loss already be zero?

No. Corresponding image locations still have different RGB values. L1 detects the mismatch, and SSIM also responds to displaced local structure.

--- ## 9. Adaptive density control: clone, split, or prune ![Cloning, splitting, and removing Gaussian primitives](assets/densification.svg) **Who makes the decision?** The authors programmed explicit heuristics in the training code. Adam does not autonomously decide how many Gaussians the scene should contain. The optimizer updates existing numerical parameters, while a **periodic density-control procedure** can alter the population of Gaussians. ### 9.1 The statistic behind the decision For Gaussian $i$ in a sampled camera, the renderer exposes its projected center $(u_i,v_i)$. Backpropagation produces the gradient of the loss with respect to that projected center: $$ g_i^{(v)}=\left\lVert\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal L_v}{\partial u_i}, \frac{\partial\mathcal L_v}{\partial v_i}\right)\right\rVert_2. $$ The code accumulates those magnitudes for visible Gaussians across training views and uses the average $$ \bar g_i=\frac{\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_i}g_i^{(v)}}{|\mathcal V_i|}. $$ A large $\bar g_i$ says that the image loss is **sensitive to changes in this Gaussian's projected position**. It does not mean the Gaussian belongs to an incorrectly segmented object or necessarily has the largest RGB loss by itself. ### 9.2 The clone/split decision rules For illustration, let $E$ be the scene extent estimated from the cameras and let $s_{\max,i}$ be the Gaussian's largest activated scale. With reference defaults, - Screen-space gradient threshold: $\tau_g=0.0002$. - Small-versus-large scale boundary: $s_{\mathrm{cut}}=0.01E$. - Low-opacity pruning threshold: $o_{\mathrm{min}}=0.005$. The main conditions are: | Condition | Action | Does the original remain? | |---|---|---| | $\bar g_i\geq\tau_g$ and $s_{\max,i}\leq 0.01E$ | **Clone**: add one copy of the small Gaussian | Yes | | $\bar g_i\geq\tau_g$ and $s_{\max,i}>0.01E$ | **Split**: create two smaller Gaussians near the parent | No, parent is removed | | Activated opacity $o_i<0.005$ | **Prune**: delete Gaussian | No | | Otherwise | **Keep** and optimize the existing Gaussian | Yes | **The real routine is staged, not a single `if/elif` statement.** It runs cloning and splitting passes and then evaluates pruning for the resulting population. It may additionally remove Gaussians that are too large in screen or world space after a size threshold is enabled. The simulation below deliberately shows the main simplified decision. ### Interactive density-control simulator Would the algorithm retain, clone, split, or prune this Gaussian?

Illustrative scene extent E = 10 world units. The small/large boundary is therefore 0.1. Adjust the quantities used by the reference heuristics.

Pruning and size checks in the real code can override a clone/split example. This simulator is a teaching aid, not a preview of the exact training trajectory.

### 9.3 What happens during cloning, splitting, and pruning? **Clone:** one additional Gaussian begins with the same position, SH coefficients, shape, opacity, and rotation as the chosen small Gaussian. The old Gaussian remains. Each subsequently has independently optimized parameters. **Split:** the reference code samples two offsets using the parent's activated scale and rotation; it creates two child Gaussians nearby and removes the parent. For the usual two-way split it sets each child's activated scale to approximately the parent's scale divided by $0.8\times2=1.6$. Copied appearance and opacity attributes can then be refined separately. **Prune:** the code deletes the selected Gaussian's parameter rows, updates the optimizer parameter tensors/state accordingly, and no longer renders it. Other Gaussians may still explain the same image region. **Merge:** a merge/combine operation is **not** part of this standard Vanilla 3DGS density-control routine. When a large Gaussian is split, it is *replaced*, not merged. ### 9.4 When do these rules run? For a typical reference 30,000-iteration configuration: | Default | Value | Meaning | |---|---:|---| | `densify_from_iter` | 500 | Densification checks begin after this iteration | | `densification_interval` | 100 | Check periodically while enabled | | `densify_until_iter` | 15,000 | Densification ends before this iteration | | `densify_grad_threshold` | 0.0002 | Threshold on averaged view-space position-gradient magnitude | | `opacity_reset_interval` | 3,000 | Periodic opacity reset | | `percent_dense` | 0.01 | Scale threshold as a fraction of scene extent | The opacity reset is **not pruning**: it caps activated opacities at 0.01, after which training can increase them again. When size pruning is enabled in the reference code, Gaussians that are too large on screen (more than 20 pixels of recorded radius) or in world space (largest scale more than 0.1 times scene extent) may also be removed. Your model's growth from **38,558 initial Gaussians** to **637,141** is the result of this population-management process together with optimization—not because the method creates one Gaussian for every pixel. ## 10. Inside one optimization iteration To understand the exact division of labor, track one iteration from beginning to end: 
Choose a registered camera and its original RGB image
         ↓
Compute Gaussian position, covariance, SH color, opacity
         ↓
Project → assign Gaussians to image tiles → sort references
         ↓
For each pixel, blend relevant Gaussians front to back
         ↓
Render RGB image at the chosen camera viewpoint
         ↓
Compare with the fixed original photograph (L1 + SSIM)
         ↓
Backpropagate through the renderer
         ↓
Accumulate position-gradient statistics for density control
         ↓
When scheduled: clone / split / prune and reset opacity
         ↓
Optimizer step on the current trainable Gaussian parameters
         ↓
Repeat for another training camera
The update paths are related but different: - **Gradient descent / Adam:** adjusts numerical values on the current Gaussian parameter tensors. - **Adaptive density control:** adds or deletes parameter rows according to rules and their accumulated statistics. - **Tile rasterization:** efficiently computes pixels and gradients from the current collection without changing how many Gaussians exist. ### Interactive full-pipeline review [Open the full pipeline explorer separately](assets/3dgs_pipeline_explorer.html). *The pipeline visualization is a guided numerical model, not the full CUDA implementation.* ## 11. The trained model: understanding the PLY file ![Trained PLY representation and resulting camera renderings](assets/ply-render-view.svg) A trained standard degree-3 Vanilla PLY includes **62 floating-point fields** per Gaussian in the reference format: | Field group | Number | What it is | |---|---:|---| | `x`, `y`, `z` | 3 | 3D Gaussian center | | `nx`, `ny`, `nz` | 3 | Normal placeholders (zeros in the official export) | | `f_dc_0` ... `f_dc_2` | 3 | Constant SH color coefficients | | `f_rest_0` ... `f_rest_44` | 45 | Higher-order SH color coefficients | | `opacity` | 1 | Stored opacity logit | | `scale_0` ... `scale_2` | 3 | Stored log-scales | | `rot_0` ... `rot_3` | 4 | Stored quaternion (normalized for rendering) | | **Total** | **62** | **59 meaningful trained values + 3 placeholders** | **The model PLY is not a checkpoint with optimizer state**. In the reference training pipeline, a separate checkpoint can also retain the optimizer and other training state. And a conventional point-cloud viewer may not know how to interpret the SH coefficients and Gaussian-specific scale/opacity conventions. ## 12. Experiments with a real trained scene This section uses your **actual trained PLY**. Python notebook cells are optional: the rest of the page is understandable without running them. The scripts `scripts/inspect_gaussians.py`, `scripts/inspect_colmap.py`, and `scripts/generate_figures.py` can also live in the website repository's root `scripts/` directory; they are not required by the browser page. ### 12.1 Count and inspect the trained Gaussians 
from plyfile import PlyData
import numpy as np

ply_path = r"3dgs_outputs_no sam/my_first_scene/point_cloud/iteration_30000/point_cloud.ply"
ply = PlyData.read(ply_path)
vtx = ply["vertex"].data

print("Trained Gaussians:", len(vtx))  # Indoor example: 637141
print("Stored properties:", len(vtx.dtype.names))
print(vtx.dtype.names)

idx = 0
center = np.array([vtx[k][idx] for k in ("x", "y", "z")])
scales = np.exp([vtx[f"scale_{k}"][idx] for k in range(3)])
opacity = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-float(vtx["opacity"][idx])))
q = np.array([vtx[f"rot_{k}"][idx] for k in range(4)])
q /= np.linalg.norm(q)

print("Gaussian", idx)
print("Center:", center)
print("Activated scales:", scales)
print("Activated opacity:", opacity)
print("Normalized quaternion (w,x,y,z):", q)
Notice that different Gaussians can have dramatically different **scales, thicknesses, and opacities**, even though they were all initialized from the same reconstruction strategy. ### 12.2 Draw one Gaussian's ellipsoid Use $\boldsymbol\mu$, $R$, and activated scales from the previous cell. Every point $\mathbf u$ on a unit sphere can be mapped to an ellipsoid surface by $$ \mathbf x=\boldsymbol\mu+R\operatorname{diag}(s_x,s_y,s_z)\mathbf u. $$ This is a one-standard-deviation **level surface** of the Gaussian distribution; plotting it provides a shape visualization, not a complete rasterized image. The plot can use `matplotlib` or `plotly`. A Gaussian may look very thin, stretched, or tilted depending on its scales and orientation. ### 12.3 Show a Gaussian projected into the camera image The official model directory often contains `cameras.json`. The path used in this example is: 
cameras_json_path = r"3dgs_outputs_no sam/my_first_scene/cameras.json"
Given a camera center $\mathbf C$ and camera-to-world rotation $R_{cw}$, the camera-space center is $\boldsymbol\mu_c=R_{cw}^\top(\boldsymbol\mu-\mathbf C)$. Then use the projection and Jacobian from [Section 4](#4-projecting-a-3d-gaussian-to-2d) to display its 2D covariance ellipse. Try several Gaussians in the **same camera**, then one Gaussian in **several cameras**. !!! warning "Visible center is not guaranteed visible surface" A projected center inside the image only means it is inside the camera's image bounds; another foreground Gaussian may still occlude it. A 2D ellipse plot does not reproduce full visibility or compositing. ### 12.4 Evaluate learned degree-3 SH coefficients This compact notebook example reads one Gaussian's complete stored appearance representation. It evaluates **all 16 degree-3 basis functions** using the official repository's helper rather than copying SH formulas by hand: 
import numpy as np
import torch
from utils.sh_utils import eval_sh   # Run in the original Gaussian-Splatting repo environment

idx = 0
sh_dc = np.array([vtx[f"f_dc_{k}"][idx] for k in range(3)])
sh_rest = np.array([vtx[f"f_rest_{k}"][idx] for k in range(45)]).reshape(3, 15)
sh = np.concatenate((sh_dc[:, None], sh_rest), axis=1)  # (3, 16)

# Illustrative unit camera-to-Gaussian direction (replace with real camera direction)
direction = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
color = eval_sh(3, torch.tensor(sh, dtype=torch.float32),
                torch.tensor(direction, dtype=torch.float32))
rgb = torch.clamp_min(color + 0.5, 0.0).numpy()
print("Direction-dependent RGB:", rgb)
If you run this notebook **outside** the `gaussian-splatting` repository, `utils.sh_utils` may not be on `PYTHONPATH`. Run it from the official repo or import that helper explicitly. To compare viewpoints, compute each camera-to-Gaussian direction as $\mathbf d=(\boldsymbol\mu-\mathbf C)/\lVert\boldsymbol\mu-\mathbf C\rVert$. ### 12.5 What to look for, beyond one Gaussian 1. Try Gaussian indices 0, 100, 1,000, and 50,000; compare activated scales and opacity. 2. Draw one Gaussian in 3D; inspect its projection into different cameras. 3. Compare SH degree 0 against degree 3 for different viewing directions. 4. Render a complete RGB image with the official renderer and inspect which structures still show artifacts. **Do not confuse per-Gaussian appearance with final rendered pixel RGB**: the latter is an ordered composition of many contributions. ## 13. Limitations and common misconceptions | Tempting assumption | More precise interpretation | |---|---| | "Each Gaussian is one pixel." | Each 3D primitive can influence many pixels and appears in many views. | | "A Gaussian is a little solid ellipsoid." | An ellipsoid is a visualization of a continuous influence function. | | "Its opacity is the alpha of all its pixels." | Pixel alpha also depends on projected footprint weight. | | "Sorting happens once for all cameras." | The relevant tile lists and depth order change with camera. | | "Training directly modifies the rendered image." | The image is recomputed from modified Gaussian parameters. | | "Adam chooses to clone or split." | Explicit density-control heuristics manage primitive counts. | | "Splitting combines several Gaussians." | Splitting replaces one large Gaussian with smaller primitives; there is no default merge step. | | "A PLY file is equivalent to a PNG or OBJ mesh." | A Gaussian PLY stores trainable scene attributes, including SH and transformed parameters. | | "High PSNR proves the geometry is correct." | RGB quality alone cannot guarantee accurate geometry or unseen views. | | "The model knows what the chair is." | Vanilla 3DGS learns appearance and spatial representation; it does not directly produce object-instance semantics. | ### Check yourself 1. If one Gaussian overlaps six tiles, how many Gaussians does the scene gain?

Zero. Tile overlap creates six references to the same primitive for image rendering, not six new trainable primitives.

2. A Gaussian has a high average projected-position gradient but is small. What will the main densification rule do?

It can clone the Gaussian. The original remains; the new copy adds representation capacity for later optimization.

3. Why does the same trained Gaussian produce different colors when the camera moves?

Its SH coefficients stay fixed, but the viewing direction changes, changing the values of the directional SH basis functions.

4. If the foreground effective alpha is 0.8, what fraction of the background contribution can pass through?

The foreground leaves 0.2 transmittance. Additional farther Gaussians may reduce it further before the background is included.

## Primary sources - Kerbl et al., [*3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04079), ACM TOG 2023. - Official [3DGS repository](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting): [`train.py`](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting/blob/main/train.py), [`scene/gaussian_model.py`](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting/blob/main/scene/gaussian_model.py), [`utils/sh_utils.py`](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting/blob/main/utils/sh_utils.py). - Official [differentiable Gaussian rasterizer](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/diff-gaussian-rasterization): [`cuda_rasterizer/rasterizer_impl.cu`](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/diff-gaussian-rasterization/blob/main/cuda_rasterizer/rasterizer_impl.cu), [`cuda_rasterizer/forward.cu`](https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/diff-gaussian-rasterization/blob/main/cuda_rasterizer/forward.cu). - Zwicker et al. (2002), [*EWA Splatting*](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2002.1031354), for the underlying footprint-filtering ideas. --- **Next reading:** [3DGS Fundamentals](fundamentals.md) if you want the concise mental picture again, or the forthcoming **Feature 3DGS** chapter for 2D-to-3D feature distillation. The separate comparison chapter will follow once both method chapters are complete.
